claim: Dyneins are motor proteins responsible for transport in the cytoplasm and the beating of axonemes in cilia and flagella.
source: Dyneins are motor proteins responsible for transport in the cytoplasm and the beating of axonemes in cilia and flagella.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about dynein function.

claim: Dyneins bind and release microtubules via a compact microtubule-binding domain (MTBD) at the end of a coiled-coil stalk.
source: They bind and release microtubules via a compact microtubule-binding domain (MTBD) at the end of a coiled-coil stalk.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynein structure and function.

claim: The majority of the MTBD is rigid upon binding, with the transition to the high-affinity state controlled by the movement of a single helix at the MTBD interface.
source: The majority of the MTBD is rigid upon binding, with the transition to the high-affinity state controlled by the movement of a single helix at the MTBD interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript, particularly the comparison of high and low affinity states shown in Figure 2.

claim: DNAH7 contains an 18-residue insertion, found in many axonemal dyneins, that contacts the adjacent protofilament.
source: DNAH7 contains an 18-residue insertion, found in many axonemal dyneins, that contacts the adjacent protofilament.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and sequence alignments presented in the manuscript, particularly Figure 3.

claim: DNAH7, but not dynein-1, induces large distortions in the microtubule cross-sectional curvature.
source: Unexpectedly, we observe that DNAH7, but not dynein-1, induces large distortions in the microtubule cross-sectional curvature.
evidence: This is supported by the structural analysis and measurements presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Dynein coordination in axonemes may be mediated via conformational changes in the microtubule.
source: This raises the possibility that dynein coordination in axonemes is mediated via conformational changes in the microtubule.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed microtubule distortions.

claim: The two cytoplasmic dyneins (dynein-1 and dynein-2) are involved in long-range movement of cellular cargoes.
source: The two cytoplasmic dyneins (dynein-1 and dynein-2) are involved in long-range movement of cellular cargoes (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Multiple inner and outer arm axonemal dyneins power the beating motion in cilia and flagella by sliding adjacent doublet microtubules past each other.
source: Multiple inner and outer arm axonemal dyneins power the beating motion in cilia and flagella by sliding adjacent doublet microtubules past each other (Satir et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: All dynein family members share a common architecture, based around a heavy chain that contains a cargo-binding tail region and a force-generating motor domain.
source: All dynein family members share a common architecture, based around a heavy chain that contains a cargo-binding tail region and a force-generating motor domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynein structure.

claim: The motor consists of a ring of six connected AAA+ subdomains (AAA1-6) with the nucleotide cycle of the first, AAA1, powering movement.
source: The motor consists of a ring of six connected AAA+ subdomains (AAA1-6) with the nucleotide cycle of the first, AAA1, powering movement (Schmidt and Carter, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The MTBD consists of six short helices (H1-H6).
source: Dyneins bind to microtubules via a small microtubule-binding domain (MTBD) consisting of six short helices (H1-H6) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1A and established knowledge.

claim: The MTBD is connected to the AAA+ ring by an antiparallel coiled-coil stalk, containing helices CC1 and CC2.
source: The MTBD is connected to the AAA +ring by an antiparallel coiled-coil stalk, containing helices CC1 and CC2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynein structure.

claim: The MTBD binds to the microtubule at the tubulin intradimer interface.
source: It binds to the microtubule at the tubulin intradimer interface (Carter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The stalk transmits conformational changes due to its ability to pack into two stable registries (α and β+), representing a half-heptad shift of CC1 relative to CC2.
source: The stalk transmits these conformational changes due to its ability to pack into two stable registries (α and β+), representing a half-heptad shift of CC1 relative to CC2 (Carter et al., 2008; Gibbons et al., 2005; Kon et al., 2009; Kon et al., 2012; Schmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The structure of the MTBD in the low microtubule affinity state (stalk in β+ registry) has been solved to high-resolution.
source: The structure of the MTBD in the low microtubule affinity state (stalk in β +registry) has been solved to high-resolution (Carter et al., 2008; Nishikawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The relative movement of CC1 towards the ring (stalk in α registry) pulls on the MTBD to create a high-affinity state.
source: The relative movement of CC1 towards the ring (stalk in α registry) pulls on the MTBD to create a high-affinity state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the dynein mechanism.

claim: The structure of the high-affinity state was visualised in a 9.7 Å cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the MTBD bound to microtubules.
source: The structure of this state was visualised in a landmark 9.7 Å cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the MTBD bound to microtubules (Redwine et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A pseudoatomic model fit into the 9.7 Å cryo-EM map using molecular dynamic simulations showed large conformational changes throughout the MTBD upon binding.
source: A pseudoatomic model was fit into the cryo-EM map using molecular dynamic simulations, and showed large conformational changes throughout the MTBD upon binding.
evidence: This is a description of previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Specific interactions between the microtubule and H1, H3, and H6 of the MTBD are required to induce and maintain the high-affinity conformation according to the previous 9.7 Å structure.
source: The authors concluded that specific interactions between the microtubule and H1, H3, and H6 of the MTBD are required to induce and maintain this high-affinity conformation.
evidence: This is a description of conclusions from previous work.

claim: A high degree of conservation in the MTBD between the different dynein family members suggests that the mechanism of microtubule binding is conserved.
source: A high degree of conservation in the MTBD between the different dynein family members suggests that this mechanism of microtubule binding is conserved (Höök and Vallee, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Many axonemal dyneins have an insertion between H2 and H3 called the flap.
source: However, many axonemal dyneins have an insertion between H2 and H3 called the flap, the function of which is unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axonemal dynein structure.

claim: An NMR structure of the Chlamydomonas reinhardtii flagellar dynein-c MTBD showed that the flap consists of two flexible beta-strands extending from the MTBD core.
source: An NMR structure of the Chlamydomonas reinhardtii flagellar dynein-c MTBD showed that the flap consists of two flexible beta-strands extending from the MTBD core (Kato et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The flap was predicted to sterically clash with the microtubule surface, and therefore undergo rearrangement upon binding.
source: The flap was predicted to sterically clash with the microtubule surface, and therefore undergo rearrangement upon binding.
evidence: This is a description of a prediction from previous work.

claim: The structure of mouse cytoplasmic dynein-1 MTBD on microtubules was determined to an overall resolution of 4.1 Å.
source: We determined the structure of mouse cytoplasmic dynein-1 MTBD on microtubules to an overall resolution of 4.1 Å.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in the manuscript, particularly Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: The transition from a low- to high-affinity state is based only around movement of H1 to avoid steric clashes with the microtubule surface.
source: This leads to an updated model for the transition from a low- to high-affinity state, based only around movement of H1 to avoid steric clashes with the microtubule surface.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The structure of microtubules decorated with the MTBD of the human inner-arm dynein DNAH7 was determined to 4.5 Å resolution.
source: Furthermore, we determine the structure of microtubules decorated with the MTBD of the human inner-arm dynein DNAH7 to 4.5 Å resolution.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in the manuscript, particularly Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The flap of DNAH7 contacts an adjacent protofilament from the rest of the MTBD.
source: We show that its flap contacts an adjacent protofilament from the rest of the MTBD, and show that this interaction dramatically distorts the microtubule cross-sectional shape.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The flap interaction dramatically distorts the microtubule cross-sectional shape.
source: We show that its flap contacts an adjacent protofilament from the rest of the MTBD, and show that this interaction dramatically distorts the microtubule cross-sectional shape.
evidence: This is supported by the structural analysis presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Predominantly 13-protofilament microtubules were made by polymerizing tubulin in an MES-based buffer.
source: Predominantly 13-protofilament microtubules were made by polymerizing tubulin in an MES-based buffer (Pierson et al., 1978).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, supported by a citation.

claim: Most microtubule architectures, including 13-protofilament microtubules, have a seam of heterotypic α-to-β contacts.
source: Microtubules are characterised by having like-for-like lateral contacts (i.e. α-to-α tubulin contacts); however, most microtubule architectures, including 13-protofilament microtubules, break this pattern with a seam of heterotypic α-to-β contacts (Desai and Mitchison, 1997) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and illustrated in a figure.

claim: Microtubules with a seam cannot be subjected to conventional helical symmetry averaging.
source: As such, these microtubules cannot be subjected to conventional helical symmetry averaging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural properties of microtubules.

claim: An alternative image processing approach integrated into the helical Relion pipeline was used for processing microtubules with a seam.
source: We propose an alternative image processing approach that is integrated into the helical Relion pipeline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, He and Scheres, 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The seam is well defined in the asymmetric reconstruction, with α-tubulins making lateral contact with β-tubulins.
source: The seam is well defined in the resulting asymmetric reconstruction, with α-tubulins making lateral contact with β-tubulins.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E/F.

claim: Application of local symmetry resulted in a map with an overall resolution of 4.1 Å for the cytoplasmic dynein-1 MTBD structure.
source: Application of local symmetry resulted in a map with an overall resolution of 4.1 Å (Figure 1C/D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the resolution data presented in the figures.

claim: The resolution of the tubulin density ranges from 3.6 Å to 4.4 Å.
source: The resolution of the tubulin density ranges from 3.6 Å to 4.4 Å (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the local resolution data shown in the figures.

claim: The tubulin model refined into the density closely matched a previous high-resolution EM model of taxol-stabilised microtubules.
source: The tubulin model refined into our density closely matched a previous high-resolution EM model of taxol-stabilised microtubules (Kellogg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work supported by a citation.

claim: The density for the dynein MTBD ranges from 4.4 Å to 8 Å in resolution.
source: The density for the dynein MTBD ranges from 4.4 Å to 8 Å in resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the local resolution data shown in the figure.

claim: Regions of the MTBD close to the microtubule were of sufficient resolution to see the pitch of alpha helices.
source: Regions of the MTBD close to the microtubule were of sufficient resolution to see the pitch of alpha helices (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the density shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The majority of the MTBD undergoes remarkably few changes upon microtubule binding when comparing the low-affinity crystal structure to the new high-affinity structure.
source: Surprisingly, when comparing the low-affinity crystal structure (Carter et al., 2008) to our new high-affinity structure, we see that the majority of the MTBD undergoes remarkably few changes upon microtubule binding (Figure 2A/B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 2A/B.

claim: The Cα RMSD between the low-affinity and high-affinity structures for helices H2 to H6 is 1.9 Å.
source: The Cα RMSD between the two structures for helices H2 to H6 is 1.9 Å.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural comparison.

claim: The major movement involves H1 and CC1, which move together to occupy the intra-dimer cleft above α- and β-tubulin.
source: The major movement involves H1 and CC1, which move together to occupy the intra-dimer cleft above α- and β-tubulin.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A more minor change is seen in H6 in order to accommodate its interaction with α-tubulin.
source: A more minor change is seen in H6 in order to accommodate its interaction with α-tubulin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The previous 9.7 Å microtubule-bound model shows H1 moving towards β-tubulin and shifting H2, H3 and H4 as a result.
source: This is in contrast to the previous 9.7 Å microtubule-bound model, in which H1 moves towards β-tubulin and shifts H2, H3 and H4 as a result (Figure 2C/D, Cα RMSD H2-H6 3.7 Å).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous structural work.

claim: The Cα RMSD for helices H2-H6 between the low-affinity structure and the previous 9.7 Å model is 3.7 Å.
source: This is in contrast to the previous 9.7 Å microtubule-bound model, in which H1 moves towards β-tubulin and shifts H2, H3 and H4 as a result (Figure 2C/D, Cα RMSD H2-H6 3.7 Å).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural comparison.

claim: A human cytoplasmic dynein-1 motor domain construct (DYNC1H11230-4646) bound to microtubules was imaged to confirm the structure is representative of full-length dynein.
source: To confirm that the structure we observed is representative of full-length dynein bound to microtubules, we imaged a human cytoplasmic dynein-1 motor domain construct (DYNC1H11230-4646, Steinman et al., 2017) bound to microtubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of an additional experiment performed to validate the findings.

claim: An overall resolution of 5.5 Å was achieved for the DYNC1H11230-4646 structure using the Relion pipeline.
source: Using the Relion pipeline we achieved an overall resolution of 5.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the resolution data presented in the figures and table.

claim: Lower microtubule occupancy was observed for DYNC1H11230-4646 compared to SRS-DYNC1H13260-3427, likely due to steric clashes between adjacent motor domains around the microtubule.
source: Lower microtubule occupancy was observed for DYNC1H11230-4646 compared to SRS-DYNC1H13260-3427, which is likely a result of steric clashes between adjacent motor domains around the microtubule.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an inference about the cause.

claim: The DYNC1H11230-4646 map fits well with the new model, but H1, H2, H3 and H4 from the 9.7 Å model are all at least partially outside the density.
source: The resulting map fits well with our new model, but H1, H2, H3 and H4 from the 9.7 Å model are all at least partially outside the density (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This is supported by the model-to-map fitting shown in the figures.

claim: Model-to-map FSC measurements indicate that the new model is a better fit to the map than the 9.7 Å model (FSC0.5=8.66 Å vs 12.76 Å).
source: Accordingly, model-to-map FSC measurements indicate that our new model is a better fit to the map (FSC0.5=8.66 Å (New model) and 12.76 Å (9.7 Å model) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model quality supported by FSC measurements.

claim: The 4.1 Å structure corresponds to the native state of the dynein MTBD bound to microtubules.
source: As such, we conclude that our 4.1 Å structure corresponds to the native state of the dynein MTBD bound to microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison with the full-length motor domain structure.

claim: The MTBD residues forming the interface with the microtubule in the new model are consistent with previous structural and mutagenesis data.
source: The MTBD residues forming the interface with the microtubule in our new model are consistent with previous structural and mutagenesis data (Gibbons et al., 2005; Koonce and Tikhonenko, 2000; Redwine et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work supported by citations.

claim: Some of the residues on the microtubule previously predicted to interact with the MTBD are too distant in the new model.
source: In contrast, some of the residues on the microtubule previously predicted to interact with the MTBD (Redwine et al., 2012) are too distant in our model (Red bonds, Figure 2—figure supplement 2G/H).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous predictions showing discrepancies.

claim: K3299 is now over 7 Å away from its previously predicted interaction partner β-tubulin E420, but is directly proximal to D427.
source: For example, K3299 is now over 7 Å away from its previously predicted interaction partner β-tubulin E420, but is directly proximal to D427 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the new structure.

claim: The MTBD is permanently primed for microtubule binding, with the only significant conformational change being the movement of H1 upwards to accommodate the change in stalk registry.
source: Overall, our new model suggests that the MTBD is permanently primed for microtubule binding. The only significant conformational change that occurs upon binding is the movement of H1 upwards to accommodate the change in stalk registry.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural comparison data.

claim: DNAH7 is a monomeric inner arm axonemal dynein closely related to Chlamydomonas reinhardti flagellar dynein-c.
source: DNAH7 is a monomeric inner arm axonemal dynein closely related to Chlamydomonas reinhardti flagellar dynein-c (Hom et al., 2011; Wickstead and Gull, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DNAH7 is one of five human axonemal dyneins to contain a flap insert between H2 and H3 of the MTBD.
source: It is one of five human axonemal dyneins to contain a flap insert between H2 and H3 of the MTBD (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A/B)
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in the figures.

claim: DNAH7 has one of the most divergent MTBD sequences compared to cytoplasmic dynein-1.
source: It is one of five human axonemal dyneins to contain a flap insert between H2 and H3 of the MTBD (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A/B), and has one of the most divergent MTBD sequences compared to cytoplasmic dynein-1.
evidence: This is an inference from sequence comparison data.

claim: A previous NMR study of Chlamydomonas flagellar dynein-c reported a low microtubule affinity.
source: A previous NMR study of Chlamydomonas flagellar dynein-c reported a low microtubule affinity (Kato et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of previous work supported by a citation.

claim: Single dynein-c molecules bind well enough to move along microtubules according to another study.
source: In contrast, another study observed that single dynein-c molecules bind well enough to move along microtubules (Sakakibara et al., 1999)
evidence: This is a description of previous work supported by a citation.

claim: An artificial construct fusing the DNAH7 MTBD onto a cytoplasmic dynein-1 stalk bound to microtubules with high-affinity.
source: an artificial construct fusing the DNAH7 MTBD onto a cytoplasmic dynein-1 stalk bound to microtubules with high-affinity (Imai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of previous work supported by a citation.

claim: An SRS-fusion containing the mouse cytoplasmic dynein-1 stalk and the human DNAH7 MTBD (SRS+-DNAH72758-2896) exhibited strong decoration of microtubules in cryo-electron micrographs.
source: Consistent with (Imai et al., 2015) this construct (SRS+-DNAH72758-2896) exhibited strong decoration of microtubules in cryo-electron micrographs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: A 4.5 Å resolution map was obtained for the DNAH7 MTBD structure following 3D classification and refinement.
source: Following 3D classification and refinement, we obtained a 4.5 Å resolution map (Figure 3B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the resolution data presented in the figures.

claim: Comparing the final microtubule-bound DNAH7 model to the original low-affinity structure shows the same conformational changes as for SRS-DYNC1H13260-3427.
source: Comparing the final microtubule-bound model to the original low-affinity structure, we observe the same conformational changes as for SRS-DYNC1H13260-3427 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a comparison of structural data.

claim: The majority of the DNAH7 MTBD remains unchanged upon binding, but H1 and CC1 move up into a raised position over the intradimer interface.
source: Namely, the majority of the MTBD remains unchanged, but H1 and CC1 move up into a raised position over the intradimer interface.
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Aligning the cytoplasmic dynein-1 model to the DNAH7 model shows that they adopt almost identical conformations.
source: Furthermore, aligning our cytoplasmic dynein-1 model to the DNAH7 model shows that they adopt almost identical conformations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a comparison of structural data.

claim: At lower threshold levels an elongated density emerges from the DNAH7 MTBD and contacts the adjacent protofilament.
source: At lower threshold levels an elongated density emerges from the DNAH7 MTBD and contacts the adjacent protofilament (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: There are two contacts between the flap and the adjacent protofilament, corresponding to H10 of β-tubulin and loop H6/7 of α-tubulin.
source: There are two contacts between the flap and this protofilament, corresponding to H10 of β-tubulin and loop H6/7 of α-tubulin (Figure 3F/G).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the figures.

claim: DNAH7 contacts four tubulin subunits at once when it binds to the microtubule.
source: As such, DNAH7 contacts four tubulin subunits at once when it binds to the microtubule.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data showing contacts with multiple tubulin subunits.

claim: The flap has a degree of flexibility based on its appearance only at lower threshold levels.
source: On account of its appearance only at lower threshold levels, we conclude that the flap has a degree of flexibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the density characteristics.

claim: The DNAH7 MTBD is tilted relative to cytoplasmic dynein when the tubulin is aligned.
source: Aligning the tubulin of the DNAH7 and cytoplasmic dynein-1 models reveals that the DNAH7 MTBD is tilted relative to cytoplasmic dynein (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural comparison shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The tilt of DNAH7 can be described by a 7° rotation around the microtubule contact site at the base of H6.
source: This can be described by a 7° rotation around the microtubule contact site at the base of H6.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural comparison.

claim: DNAH7 is tilted in the same direction as the flap, suggesting that its interaction with the adjacent protofilament pulls on the entire MTBD.
source: DNAH7 is tilted in the same direction as the flap, suggesting that its interaction with the adjacent protofilament pulls on the entire MTBD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: An additional link between the DNAH7 MTBD and the adjacent protofilament was revealed by lowpass filtering and thresholding the map to a lower level.
source: Lowpass filtering and thresholding the map to a lower level revealed the presence of an additional link between the DNAH7 MTDB and the adjacent protofilament (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The additional density is suspected to be attributed to the β-tubulin 'E-hook' due to its proximity to the C-terminus of β-tubulin.
source: Due to its proximity to the C-terminus of β-tubulin, we suspect that this density is attributed to the β-tubulin 'E-hook'.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the location of the density.

claim: The β-tubulin E-hook is a normally unstructured ~20 residue chain of mostly glutamate residues that strongly contributes to the electronegative surface of microtubules.
source: This is a normally unstructured ~20 residue chain of mostly glutamate residues that strongly contributes to the electronegative surface of microtubules (Nogales et al., 1998; Redeker et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The same link is not observed in the cytoplasmic dynein-1 density at any threshold.
source: We note that the same link is not observed in our cytoplasmic dynein-1 density (Figure 3I) at any threshold.
evidence: This is a comparison of the two structures.

claim: DNAH7 has a large positively charged patch on the top of the MTBD that is absent in cytoplasmic dynein-1.
source: Examination of the surface charges of our two models reveals a large positively charged patch on the top of the DNAH7 MTBD that is absent in cytoplasmic dynein-1 (Figure 3J/K).
evidence: This is a comparison of the electrostatic properties of the two models.

claim: Modelling of the β-tubulin E-hook shows that it is capable of reaching the positively charged patch on DNAH7.
source: Modelling of the β-tubulin E-hook show that it is capable of reaching this patch.
evidence: This is a modeling result supporting the interpretation.

claim: On top of a core microtubule interaction shared with cytoplasmic dynein, DNAH7 is bolstered by two links to the adjacent protofilament.
source: As such, we conclude that on top of a core microtubule interaction shared with cytoplasmic dynein, DNAH7 is bolstered by two links to the adjacent protofilament.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural observations.

claim: The microtubule was distorted in the DNAH7 structure compared to other reconstructions.
source: During the process of solving the DNAH7 MTBD structure, we noticed that the microtubule was distorted compared to our other reconstructions.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: Initial application of local symmetry using the same operators as previous structures resulted in weaker decorating density and blurring of tubulin helices for DNAH7.
source: Initial application of local symmetry, using the same operators as our previous structures, resulted in a weaker decorating density and blurring of tubulin helices (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D/E).
evidence: This is an observation from the image processing.

claim: The averaging between different protofilaments was incoherent, suggesting the cross-section of the microtubule was distorted.
source: This suggested that the averaging between different protofilaments was incoherent, and the cross-section of the microtubule was distorted.
evidence: This is an inference based on the image processing results.

claim: Relion was used to refine the local symmetry operators, which improved the features and led to the final 4.5 Å map.
source: We therefore used Relion to refine the local symmetry operators, which improved the features and led to our final 4.5 Å map (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a description of the methodological approach.

claim: Measurements for the SRS-DYNC1H13260-3427 map showed the angle between each protofilament close to 27.69° (S.D. = 0.17°).
source: Measurements for the SRS-DYNC1H13260-3427 map were as expected, with the angle between each protofilament close to 27.69° (360°/13 protofilaments, S.D. = 0.17°) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural analysis.

claim: The refined SRS+-DNAH72758-2896 structure exhibited protofilament angles ranging from 26.5° to 28.7° (S.D = 0.75°).
source: In contrast, our refined SRS+-DNAH72758-2896 structure exhibited protofilament angles ranging from 26.5° to 28.7° (S.D = 0.75°, Figure 4B)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural analysis.

claim: The protofilament angle variations in DNAH7 represent large changes in the local curvature of the microtubule.
source: In contrast, our refined SRS+-DNAH72758-2896 structure exhibited protofilament angles ranging from 26.5° to 28.7° (S.D = 0.75°, Figure 4B), representing large changes in the local curvature of the microtubule.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quantitative measurements.

claim: Reclassification of the SRS+-DNAH72758-2896 data with modified classification parameters resulted in two extreme classes, 'A' and 'B', with large differences in cross-sectional curvature.
source: However, to investigate the curvature further, we reclassified the SRS+-DNAH72758-2896 data with modified classification parameters (see Materials and methods, Figure 3—figure supplement 2H). This resulted in two extreme classes, 'A' and 'B', with large differences in cross-sectional curvature (Figure 4C, Video 1).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis and its results.

claim: The formation of multiple good classes indicates that the microtubules in the DNAH7 dataset form a continuous distribution of distorted curvatures.
source: The formation of multiple good classes indicates that the microtubules in this dataset form a continuous distribution of distorted curvatures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the classification results.

claim: Classes A and B had protofilament angles ranging from 25.1° to 31.8°.
source: Classes A and B had even greater local cross-sectional curvature distortions than our refined map, with protofilament angles ranging from 25.1° to 31.8° (Figure 4D/E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural analysis.

claim: The local curvatures between protofilaments resulting from DNAH7 distortions are within the range of those seen in canonical 12 and 14 protofilament microtubules.
source: The local curvatures between protofilaments that result from these distortions are thus within the range of those seen in canonical 12 (25.71°) and 14 (30°) protofilament microtubules.
evidence: This is a comparison of the measured values to known microtubule architectures.

claim: The distortions change the microtubule cross-section from a circular to an elliptical profile.
source: These distortions change the microtubule cross-section from a circular to an elliptical profile.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural measurements.

claim: The ellipticity of class A and B is 0.936 and 0.942, respectively.
source: The ellipticity (the ratio between the long and short diameters of an ellipse) of class A and B is 0.936 and 0.942, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I/J).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural analysis.

claim: The ellipticity of DNAH7-decorated microtubules is much greater than the cytoplasmic dynein-1 structure (0.995) and previous studies.
source: This is much greater than microtubule ellipticity measured both in our cytoplasmic dynein-1 structure (0.995, Figure 3—figure supplement 2K) and previous studies (Kellogg et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a comparison to the cytoplasmic dynein structure and previous work.

claim: DNAH7 is responsible for the microtubule distortion based on the ellipticity measurements.
source: This is much greater than microtubule ellipticity measured both in our cytoplasmic dynein-1 structure (0.995, Figure 3—figure supplement 2K) and previous studies (Kellogg et al., 2017), indicating that DNAH7 is responsible for this distortion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of ellipticity values.

claim: A clear correlation is observed in which the decoration is highest at low local protofilament curvatures in classes A and B.
source: We observe a clear correlation in which the decoration is highest at low local protofilament curvatures (Figure 4D/E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of decoration levels and curvature.

claim: Local curvature within sub-classes ranged from 23.6° to 32.5°.
source: Local curvature within sub-classes ranged from 23.6° to 32.5° (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the sub-classification analysis.

claim: The local curvature range highlights the structural heterogeneity within DNAH7 decorated microtubules.
source: Local curvature within sub-classes ranged from 23.6° to 32.5° (Figure 5B), highlighting the structural heterogeneity within DNAH7 decorated microtubules.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the measurement results.

claim: There is a linear relationship between decoration level and local curvature, with the lowest curvature (flattest) sub-classes having the highest decoration.
source: This shows a linear relationship between decoration level and local curvature, with the lowest curvature (flattest) sub-classes having the highest decoration.
evidence: This is supported by the plot in Figure 5C showing R² = 0.72.

claim: In all the sub-classes, there is evidence of the flap contacting the adjacent protofilament.
source: In all the sub-classes, we see evidence of the flap contacting the adjacent protofilament, suggesting that the main differences in curvature result from the degree of decoration.
evidence: This is an observation from the sub-classification analysis.

claim: The main differences in curvature result from the degree of decoration.
source: In all the sub-classes, we see evidence of the flap contacting the adjacent protofilament, suggesting that the main differences in curvature result from the degree of decoration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the flap is always present.

claim: The DNAH7 MTBD induces a local flattening of the microtubule.
source: Based on our observations, we propose that the DNAH7 MTBD induces a local flattening of the microtubule.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the curvature and decoration analysis.

claim: The pattern of decoration suggests that the DNAH7 MTBD binds more weakly to higher curvatures and more strongly to flatter curvatures.
source: The pattern of decoration suggests that the DNAH7 MTBD binds more weakly to higher curvatures and more strongly to flatter curvatures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between decoration and curvature.

claim: The flap is likely the element responsible for the microtubule flattening, given that it is the only major difference between the cytoplasmic dynein-1 and DNAH7 MTBD.
source: Given that the only major difference between the cytoplasmic dynein-1 and DNAH7 MTBD is the flap, it seems likely that this is the element responsible for the flattening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison.

claim: The observation that the flap contacts the adjacent protofilament supports that it is responsible for the flattening.
source: This is supported by our observation that the flap contacts the adjacent protofilament to the MTBDs binding site.
evidence: This is a logical connection between the structural observation and the proposed mechanism.

claim: In the DNAH7 MTBD sub-classes, there is no evidence of docked MTBDs without flap binding, suggesting that the flap contact is an integral feature of the DNAH7 microtubule interaction.
source: In our DNAH7 MTBD sub-classes (Figure 5B), we do not see any evidence of docked MTBDs without flap binding, suggesting that the flap contact is an integral feature of the DNAH7 microtubule interaction.
evidence: This is an observation from the sub-classification analysis.

claim: The movement of the MTBD towards the adjacent protofilament suggests that there is tension created by the flap.
source: Furthermore, the movement of the MTBD towards the adjacent protofilament suggests that there is tension created by the flap.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The tension created by the flap results in the relative movement between protofilaments that generates a local flattening.
source: We propose that this tension results in the relative movement between protofilaments that generates a local flattening.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The workflow for solving microtubule structures in Relion is straightforward and does not require expert knowledge.
source: The workflow we present for solving microtubule structures in Relion is straightforward and does not require expert knowledge.
evidence: This is a claim about the methodology presented in the manuscript.

claim: Re-processing EMPIAR dataset 10030 (EB3-decorated microtubules) following the Relion pipeline resulted in a 3.5 Å resolution map essentially identical to the published structure.
source: To test the general applicability for decorated microtubules, we re-processed EMPIAR dataset 10030, which comprises EB3-decorated microtubules. This data set was previously refined to 3.5 Å resolution using an iterative seam-finding protocol (Zhang and Nogales, 2015; Zhang and Nogales, 2015). Following the Relion pipeline with the same data resulted in an asymmetric map with lower levels of density on the protofilaments either side of the seam, suggesting that not all particles were aligned correctly with respect to the seam (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D/E). However, after symmetrization the map extends to 3.5 Å resolution and is essentially identical in appearance to the published structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is a validation of the method using a published dataset.

claim: Relion can be used to reconstruct pseudosymmetric microtubules and their decorating partners to high resolution.
source: We conclude that Relion can be used to reconstruct pseudosymmetric microtubules and their decorating partners to high resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful re-processing of the EB3 dataset.

claim: Many previously introduced methods for microtubule reconstruction explicitly determine and enforce a single seam orientation for each microtubule.
source: We note that many of the previously introduced methods for microtubule reconstruction explicitly determine, and enforce, a single seam orientation for each microtubule (Sindelar and Downing, 2007; Zhang and Nogales, 2015).
evidence: This is a description of previous methods supported by citations.

claim: In Relion, each segment is aligned independently from its neighbours in the same microtubule, and mistakes in alignment of the seam can be made on a per-segment basis.
source: Therefore, each segment is aligned independently from its neighbours in the same microtubule, and mistakes in alignment of the seam can be made on a per-segment basis.
evidence: This is a description of how Relion handles microtubule alignment.

claim: Relion appears to require a larger decorating density (such as the dynein MTBD) to fully align the seam, at least in its current implementation.
source: Therefore, at least in its current implementation, Relion appears to require a larger decorating density (such as the dynein MTBD) to fully align the seam.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observations from the EB3 dataset processing.

claim: The MTBD interface made up of H2, H3, H4 and H6 shows only minor changes upon microtubule binding, suggesting it is in a binding-primed conformation regardless of nucleotide state.
source: The MTBD interface made up of H2, H3, H4 and H6 shows only minor changes upon microtubule binding, suggesting it is in a binding-primed conformation regardless of nucleotide state.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural comparison.

claim: A stable microtubule-bound state cannot be achieved when dynein is in a low-affinity state due to a steric clash between H1 and β-tubulin.
source: This interface can initiate contact with the microtubule, but a stable microtubule-bound state cannot be achieved when dynein is in a low-affinity state due to a steric clash between H1 and β-tubulin.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: When the motor switches to a high microtubule affinity nucleotide state, H1 moves up and the MTBD can be further stabilised on the microtubule by interactions between H1 and β-tubulin.
source: When the motor switches to a high microtubule affinity nucleotide state, H1 moves up and the MTBD can be further stabilised on the microtubule by interactions between H1 and β-tubulin.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural data.

claim: When ATP binds to the motor, changes in the stalk push H1 down and release the MTBD from the microtubule.
source: Conversely, when ATP binds to the motor, changes in the stalk (Schmidt et al., 2015) push H1 down and release the MTBD from the microtubule.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural data and previous work.

claim: The predominant change in both the cytoplasmic dynein-1 and DNAH7 MTBDs is the position of H1, suggesting this is a conserved mechanism for controlling dynein binding to microtubules.
source: Combining our current work with previous studies (Carter et al., 2008; Kato et al., 2014), we now have structures of two distantly related dynein MTBDs both on and off the microtubule. In both the cytoplasmic dynein-1 and DNAH7 MTBDs, the predominant change is the position of H1, suggesting this is a conserved mechanism for controlling dynein binding to microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of the two structures and previous work.

claim: The addition of an extended flap between H2 and H3 in DNAH7 results in important differences to cytoplasmic dynein.
source: However, the addition of an extended flap between H2 and H3 in DNAH7 results in important differences to cytoplasmic dynein.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural comparison.

claim: The flap extends the contact area with the microtubule to include four tubulin subunits, supplementing the core interaction observed in cytoplasmic dynein-1.
source: The flap extends the contact area with the microtubule to include four tubulin subunits, supplementing the core interaction observed in cytoplasmic dynein-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data.

claim: The interaction between the flap and adjacent protofilament drives large distortions in lattice curvature.
source: We propose that this interaction drives large distortions in lattice curvature.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: A second link to the adjacent protofilament is assigned to the acidic C-terminal tail of beta-tubulin binding to a pocket of positively charged residues on the top surface of the DNAH7 MTBD.
source: We assign a second link to the adjacent protofilament to the acidic C-terminal tail of beta-tubulin binding to a pocket of positively charged residues on the top surface of the DNAH7 MTBD.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the density and electrostatic properties.

claim: The angle the stalk of DNAH7 makes relative to the microtubule is tilted in an off-axis direction compared to cytoplasmic dynein-1.
source: The angle the stalk of DNAH7 makes relative to the microtubule is tilted in an off-axis direction compared to cytoplasmic dynein-1.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural comparison.

claim: Many inner arm dyneins generate torque.
source: It is interesting to note that many inner arm dyneins generate torque (Vale and Toyoshima, 1988; Kagami and Kamiya R, 1992; Kikushima and Kamiya, 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The tilt of DNAH7 may be one mechanism that could contribute to torque generation.
source: It is interesting to note that many inner arm dyneins generate torque (Vale and Toyoshima, 1988; Kagami and Kamiya R, 1992; Kikushima and Kamiya, 2008) and we speculate that the tilt may be one mechanism that could contribute to this.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural observation.

claim: Some members of the kinesin family of microtubule motors are known to induce changes in the microtubule lattice.
source: Some members of the kinesin family of microtubule motors are known to induce changes in the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinesin motors.

claim: Kinesin-1 induces a longitudinal extension of the microtubule.
source: These include a longitudinal extension by kinesin-1 (Peet et al., 2018)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Kinesin-13 induces the peeling back of single protofilaments.
source: and the peeling back of single protofilaments by kinesin-13 (Hunter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Both kinesin-1 and kinesin-13 effects are related to the longitudinal axis, and no effects on cross-sectional curvature have been observed to date.
source: Both these effects are related to the longitudinal axis however, and no effects on cross-sectional curvature have been observed to date.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Some microtubule-associated proteins are sensitive to the lateral curvature of the microtubule.
source: In contrast, some microtubule-associated proteins are sensitive to the lateral curvature of the microtubule.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAPs.

claim: Doublecortin (DCX) and EB3 both bind in the cleft between two adjacent protofilaments and contact four tubulin subunits.
source: Doublecortin (DCX) and EB3 both bind in the cleft between two adjacent protofilaments and contact four tubulin subunits (Moores et al., 2004; Zhang and Nogales, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DCX and EB3 lateral interactions promote formation of 13-protofilament microtubules during polymerization.
source: These lateral interactions promote formation of 13-protofilament microtubules during polymerization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DCX and EB3 function.

claim: DCX and EB3 promote a rounder, more regular microtubule lattice.
source: This promotes a rounder, more regular lattice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DCX and EB3 function.

claim: DNAH7 is unusual in directly distorting the cross-sectional curvature of mature microtubules.
source: Therefore, DNAH7 is unusual in directly distorting the cross-sectional curvature of mature microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison to other microtubule-binding proteins.

claim: A number of other axonemal dyneins possess an MTBD flap.
source: A number of other axonemal dyneins possess an MTBD flap (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B/C).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment data shown in the figure.

claim: In C. reinhardtii, the γ outer arm dynein and the a, b, c, d and e inner arm dyneins all possess an 18/19-residue loop between H2 and H3.
source: In C. reinhardtii, the γ outer arm dynein and the a, b, c, d and e inner arm dyneins all possess an 18/19-residue loop between H2 and H3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment data shown in the figure.

claim: Cryo-electron tomography has mapped the position of each dynein MTBD in the axoneme.
source: Cryo-electron tomography has mapped the position of each dynein MTBD in the axoneme (Figure 6A) (Bui et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Nicastro et al., 2006; Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Microtubules in the axoneme form a doublet structure, consisting of a 13-protofilament A-tubule and a connected 10-protofilament B-tubule.
source: Microtubules in the axoneme form a doublet structure, consisting of a 13-protofilament A-tubule and a connected 10-protofilament B-tubule.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axonemal structure.

claim: The tail of axonemal dyneins dock onto the A-tubule, positioning the MTBDs to bind to an adjacent doublet B-tubule.
source: The tail of axonemal dyneins dock onto the A-tubule, positioning the MTBDs to bind to an adjacent doublet B-tubule.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axonemal dynein organization.

claim: The flap containing dyneins are spread along the length of the axonemal repeat but only contact two pairs of protofilaments on one side of the B-tubule.
source: Strikingly, the flap containing dyneins are spread along the length of the axonemal repeat but only contact two pairs of protofilaments on one side of the B-tubule (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation based on the mapping of dynein positions in the axoneme.

claim: There is one side of the B-tubule on which flap-containing dyneins act at a high local concentration.
source: As such, there is one side of the B-tubule on which flap-containing dyneins act at a high local concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of flap-containing dyneins.

claim: The effect of dynein binding to microtubules in the axoneme may result in even greater distortions than those observed in the DNAH7 decorated microtubule structure.
source: The effect of dynein binding to microtubules in the axoneme may therefore result in even greater distortions than those we observed.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the concentration of flap-containing dyneins in the axoneme.

claim: DNAH7 binding may have a different effect on axonemal doublets compared to in vitro polymerized microtubules, where inner proteins may increase the microtubule stiffness.
source: Conversely, as our study was performed on in vitro polymerized microtubules we cannot rule out that DNAH7 binding has a different effect on axonemal doublets, where for example inner proteins may increase the microtubule stiffness (Ichikawa et al., 2017; Ichikawa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledging potential differences between in vitro and in vivo conditions.

claim: Axonemal dyneins drive ciliary bending.
source: Axonemal dyneins drive ciliary bending (King, 2018; Satir et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Most models suggest that localised activation and inhibition of axonemal dyneins is needed to create the imbalance in forces across the axoneme that result in an overall bend.
source: Most models suggest that localised activation and inhibition of axonemal dyneins is needed to create the imbalance in forces across the axoneme that result in an overall bend.
evidence: This is a description of current models in the field.

claim: Models of ciliary bending rely on communication between axonemal dyneins such that they are active or inactive at the right time.
source: These models rely on communication between axonemal dyneins such that they are active or inactive at the right time.
evidence: This is a description of current models in the field.

claim: The flap could play a role in communication between axonemal dyneins.
source: We speculate that the flap could play a role in communication.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural findings.

claim: Higher decoration at lower lateral curvature suggests that the DNAH7 MTBD could act as a curvature sensor in the axoneme.
source: We observed higher decoration at lower lateral curvature in our classes (Figure 4D/E), suggesting that the DNAH7 MTBD could act as a curvature sensor in the axoneme.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the correlation between decoration and curvature.

claim: The inner proteins maintain the local curvature of the inner arm dynein binding site at ~25°, which would favour DNAH7 binding.
source: We note that the inner proteins maintain the local curvature of the inner arm dynein binding site at ~25°, which would favour DNAH7 binding (Carter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an observation connecting previous work to the current findings.

claim: The cross-section of microtubules is thought to flatten during bending.
source: The cross-section of microtubules is thought to flatten during bending (Memet et al., 2018)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: If microtubules flatten during bending, dynein binding would cyclically change during the axonemal beat.
source: The cross-section of microtubules is thought to flatten during bending (Memet et al., 2018), in which case dynein binding would cyclically change during the axonemal beat.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the curvature sensitivity of DNAH7.

claim: The flap-induced distortion of the microtubule could induce cooperative binding of adjacent dyneins, potentially helping a waveform spread through the cilium.
source: Alternatively, the flap-induced distortion of the microtubule could induce cooperative binding of adjacent dyneins, potentially helping a waveform spread through the cilium.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional role of the flap.

claim: Higher resolution structures of axonemal dyneins in the context of a ciliary beat will be required to test the hypotheses about the flap's role in dynein coordination.
source: Higher resolution structures of axonemal dyneins in the context of a ciliary beat will be required to test these hypotheses.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed to validate the speculations.
